title: Mental capacity in pregnancy and labour
blurb: Apply the Mental Capacity Act 2005 to decisions in pregnancy and labour: presume capacity, support decisions, assess properly and act in best interests.
question: A woman in the second stage of labour, exhausted and in pain, declines an assisted birth that the obstetrician recommends for fetal bradycardia. The obstetrician says 'she can't think straight, so she lacks capacity'. What should the midwife do?

teach.body: Mental capacity is the ability to make a particular decision at the time it needs to be made. The Mental Capacity Act 2005 (England and Wales) applies to decisions in pregnancy and labour just as at any other time. In plain English: every woman is assumed able to decide unless it is shown she cannot, and that is judged for this decision, now, not for her as a person. Code 4.3 asks you to keep to the capacity law of the country where you practise.
teach.cite: Mental Capacity Act 2005 ss1 to 3; NMC Code 4.3

head: s1
Principle
In labour
rows: Pain or fear is not proof she cannot decide
Least intrusive way to achieve the aim

steps.label: Impairment?
steps.sub: Of, or disturbance in, mind or brain

steps.label: Retain?
steps.sub: Long enough to decide; briefly is enough

teach.caption: If there is an impairment AND she cannot do any one of the four, she lacks capacity for that decision. It may be temporary (s2(2)).

teach.body: Pain, exhaustion, fear, Entonox or opioids may affect a woman's thinking, but none of them by itself shows she lacks capacity. s2(3) says incapacity cannot be established merely by reference to a person's condition or behaviour. The question is whether, because of an impairment, she cannot understand, retain, use or weigh, or communicate this decision. Courts have stressed that a competent pregnant woman's decision must be respected unless she lacks the legal capacity to decide.

teach.h: Scenario: Lydia in the second stage
teach.body: Lydia is exhausted and declines the ventouse the obstetrician advises for a fetal bradycardia. Her midwife, Asha, does not accept 'she can't think straight' as an assessment. Between contractions, Asha and the obstetrician explain simply what is proposed, why, the risks of each option and the alternatives. Lydia repeats back the risk to her baby, weighs it, and clearly says she wants to keep pushing for now. She has capacity; her decision stands, and the team keeps monitoring and keeps talking with her.

head: Consider
rows: Whether she may regain capacity, and when (can it wait?)
Encouraging her to participate as fully as possible
Her past and present wishes, feelings, beliefs and values (especially written statements)
The views of those close to her, and anyone she named
No decision based on age, appearance or assumptions
teach.caption: A partner cannot consent for an adult; he is consulted as part of the best interests process.

items: Capacity is presumed for women aged 16 and over; MCA powers do not apply under 16 (s2(5)).
Give information in a way suited to her: simple language, visual aids, between contractions, interpreter (s3(2)).
If capacity is temporarily lost (for example an eclamptic seizure), consider whether the decision can wait until she recovers.
Restraint is lawful under s6 only if necessary to prevent harm to her and proportionate.
Record the decision, the assessment of each ability and who was involved.

teach.text: Disagreeing with medical advice is not evidence of incapacity (s1(4)). The capacity test is about HOW she decides (understand, retain, weigh, communicate), not WHAT she decides. And capacity is decision-specific: she may be able to decide about pain relief but not, at the same moment, about a complex surgical choice, or vice versa.

items: MCA 2005 applies in England and Wales; capacity is presumed, decision-specific and time-specific.
Five principles: presume capacity, support, unwise is not incapable, best interests, less restrictive option.
Test: impairment of mind or brain plus inability to understand, retain, use or weigh, or communicate.
Labour, pain or fear alone does not remove capacity; a competent woman's refusal stands.
If she lacks capacity: advance decision, LPA, or best interests (s4); disputes go to the Court of Protection (s15).

summary: You can now apply the MCA 2005 principles and capacity test to decisions in pregnancy and labour, without confusing pain, fear or disagreement with incapacity. You can also explain what happens when a woman lacks capacity, including best interests and the Court of Protection.

A.q: Which is the first principle of the Mental Capacity Act 2005?
options: Act in the person's best interests in every case
Choose the less restrictive option for the person
Treat unwise decisions as a sign of incapacity
Assume a person has capacity unless shown otherwise
A.why: s1(2): a person must be assumed to have capacity unless it is established that they lack it.

whyNot.0: Best interests (s1(5)) applies only once incapacity is established.
whyNot.1: The less restrictive option is the fifth principle (s1(6)).
whyNot.2: s1(4) says the opposite: an unwise decision does not mean incapacity.

A.q: A woman can understand and weigh information about an epidural but forgets the details a few minutes later. Does this mean she lacks capacity?
options: Yes, she cannot retain the information
No, brief retention is enough to decide
Yes, unless her partner confirms her wishes
No, because she is over 18 years old
A.why: s3(3): being able to retain information only for a short period does not prevent a person being regarded as able to make the decision.

whyNot.0: Retaining information long enough to make the decision is sufficient.
whyNot.2: Her partner's confirmation is not part of the test.
whyNot.3: Age alone does not establish capacity.

A.q: Which statement about capacity is correct?
options: It is assessed once at booking
It applies to all decisions equally
It is specific to each decision
It is lost during established labour
A.why: s2(1): lack of capacity is about a particular matter at the material time.

whyNot.0: Capacity is assessed when a particular decision needs to be made.
whyNot.3: Labour does not of itself remove capacity.

B.q: A woman with a learning disability is offered induction. She appears unsure. What should the midwife do first?
options: Give information in a way she can understand
Ask her mother to make the decision for her
Record that she lacks capacity to decide
Make a best interests decision on her behalf
B.why: s1(3): a person is not treated as unable to decide unless all practicable steps to help her have been taken without success; s3(2): information explained in an appropriate way.

whyNot.1: Her mother cannot decide for an adult.
whyNot.2: A learning disability does not by itself mean incapacity (s2(3)).
whyNot.3: Best interests applies only once incapacity is established after support.

B.q: A woman has an eclamptic seizure and is unconscious. She needs urgent magnesium sulfate. On what legal basis is it given?
options: With her partner's consent as next of kin
Under an urgent court order from a judge
In her best interests, as she lacks capacity
Through implied consent given at booking
B.why: She lacks capacity (temporary impairment) and urgent treatment cannot wait; the team acts in her best interests under the MCA (s4, s5).

whyNot.0: A partner cannot consent for an adult (unless a health and welfare attorney).
whyNot.1: There is no time for a court order, and none is needed for urgent best interests treatment.
whyNot.3: Booking does not provide consent for emergency treatment.

B.q: A pregnant 15-year-old needs a decision about her care. Which statement about the MCA 2005 is correct?
options: Its powers apply from age 12
Its powers apply from conception
Its powers apply once she is pregnant
Its powers do not apply under 16
B.why: s2(5): powers under the Act are not exercisable in relation to a person under 16 (with limited exceptions).

whyNot.1: The Act concerns persons, not stages of fetal development.
whyNot.2: Pregnancy does not change the age threshold.

C.q: In labour, a woman declines a caesarean for suspected fetal compromise. She explains the risks to her baby accurately and says she accepts them for religious reasons. The registrar wants to proceed in her best interests. What is correct?
options: She has capacity and her refusal must be respected
She lacks capacity because her choice is risky
Best interests allows the caesarean for the baby
The Court of Protection must approve her refusal
C.why: She understands, retains, weighs and communicates: she has capacity. s1(4): an unwise decision is not incapacity; best interests does not arise. St George's v S: the baby's needs do not prevail.

whyNot.1: The risk of a choice does not establish incapacity.
whyNot.2: Best interests applies only to a person who lacks capacity.
whyNot.3: A competent refusal needs no court approval.

C.q: A woman lacks capacity because of acute psychosis late in pregnancy. A decision is needed about planned caesarean in 2 weeks. Her family strongly disagree about what she would want. What is the most appropriate step?
options: Let the family vote on what she would want
Follow the obstetrician's preferred plan of care
Wait until she is in labour and decide then
Seek legal advice about the Court of Protection
C.why: Where there is serious dispute or doubt, the Court of Protection can make declarations about capacity and the lawfulness of an act (s15). Planning ahead avoids emergency decisions.

whyNot.0: Family members are consulted but do not decide.
whyNot.1: Best interests is not the same as one professional's preference.
whyNot.2: Delaying risks an emergency decision with less time to consider her wishes.

C.q: A woman who has had pethidine is drowsy but rousable when a perineal repair is needed. What should the midwife do?
options: Assume she lacks capacity because of pethidine
Proceed, as consent was given at booking
Assess whether she can make this decision
Ask her partner to consent to the repair
C.why: Capacity is presumed and decision-specific; drowsiness after an opioid does not by itself establish incapacity. The midwife assesses the four abilities and, if needed, considers whether the repair can wait until she can decide.

whyNot.0: A drug or condition alone does not establish incapacity (s2(3)).
whyNot.1: Consent is sought for each procedure at the time.
whyNot.3: A partner cannot consent for an adult.

reteach.title: HOW she decides, not WHAT
reteach.question: When a woman's choice worries you, what exactly should you be testing?

blocks.h: Test the process, not the outcome
blocks.body: Capacity is about the process of deciding. Can she understand what is proposed and why? Can she hold on to it long enough? Can she weigh the pros and cons? Can she tell you her decision in any way? If yes to all four, she has capacity, even if her choice worries you.

blocks.text: A partner is consulted, not asked to consent. Only a valid health and welfare attorney (or the court) can decide for an adult who lacks capacity.

explain.body: s1(2) assume capacity; (3) all practicable support; (4) unwise is not incapable; (5) best interests; (6) less restrictive option.

test.q: A woman chooses to labour at home against advice. Which MCA principle reminds the midwife this does not mean she lacks capacity?
test.why: s1(4): a person is not to be treated as unable to make a decision merely because she makes an unwise decision.

whyNot.0: s1(2) is the presumption of capacity.
whyNot.3: s1(6) is the less restrictive option.

explain.body: s2: impairment of, or disturbance in, the functioning of the mind or brain, permanent or temporary. s3: unable to understand, retain, use or weigh, or communicate.

test.q: Which of these is NOT one of the four abilities in s3 of the MCA?
options: Understand the information
Retain the information
Agree with the recommendation
Communicate the decision
test.why: The four abilities are understand, retain, use or weigh, and communicate. Agreeing with advice is not required.

whyNot.0: Understanding is one of the four.
whyNot.1: Retaining is one of the four.
whyNot.3: Communicating (by any means) is one of the four.

explain.body: s4: consider whether she may regain capacity, involve her, her past and present wishes and beliefs, and consult those close to her. Not based on age, appearance or assumptions.

test.q: A woman lacks capacity after a major haemorrhage. Her partner asks to sign consent for a hysterectomy. She has no LPA. What is correct?
options: He is consulted; clinicians decide in her best interests
He can consent as her next of kin in an emergency
He can consent because they are legally married
He must apply to the Court of Protection first
test.why: Next of kin cannot consent for an adult. Without an LPA or advance decision, the treating clinician decides in her best interests, consulting her partner about her wishes (s4(7)).

whyNot.1: Next of kin has no legal power to consent for an adult.
whyNot.2: Marriage does not give power to consent.
whyNot.3: Urgent treatment in best interests does not require a court application.

explain.body: s15: the court can declare whether a person has or lacks capacity for a decision, and whether an act is lawful. Used for serious disputes or doubt, ideally planned ahead of birth.

test.q: What can the Court of Protection declare under s15 of the MCA 2005?
options: That a fetus has separate legal rights
That a midwife is unfit to practise
Whether a trust is safely staffed
Whether a person has capacity for a decision
test.why: s15(1): declarations about whether a person has or lacks capacity for a decision, and about the lawfulness of acts done or to be done.

whyNot.0: The fetus is not a separate legal person.
whyNot.1: Fitness to practise is for the NMC.
whyNot.2: Staffing is a matter for regulators such as the CQC.
